title: AI and the Fall? of the Creative Class
gist: US creative industries have lost more than 200k jobs in four years with no general recession. The damage is concentrated in Hollywood (more than 100k jobs, about a third of the sector), while in-person entertainment is still growing, which Politano reads as evidence of AI's role. Using music's piracy-to-live-touring shift and newspapers' collapse as analogies, he argues video has no live fallback, but says AI art's main effects are cultural rather than macroeconomic. He adds that broader displacement (already visible in tech) must spread if AI is to justify the trillions invested in it.

themes.theme: Creative-sector job losses in the US

insights.claim: US creative industries (media, film and the arts) have lost more than 200k jobs over the last four years, about 50k of them in the last year, a pace matched only by the 2001 and 2008 recessions.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Sector-specific labor contraction with no general recession is a sign of structural, not cyclical, displacement.
insights.quote: America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone.

insights.claim: The clearest evidence of AI's role is that every digital arts subsector is losing jobs, while in-person entertainment keeps growing at a healthy pace.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Physical/live experiences look like the AI-resistant part of entertainment; digital content is the exposed part.
insights.quote: perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.

insights.claim: Media firms underreport their AI use, both to avoid public backlash and to protect the legal basis of their copyrights, so AI-driven job loss is hard to measure directly.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Disclosed corporate AI adoption in media probably understates real use; don't rely on company statements.
insights.quote: Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights.

insights.claim: The US movie & TV industry has lost more than 100k jobs in four years, nearly one-third of the sector, and this summer's employment low was below any point since the 2008 recession, close to a 30-year low.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Legacy studio labor and cost bases are shrinking structurally; it's an industry in secular decline.
insights.quote: Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total.
insights.locator: Hollywood has never seen a stretch

insights.claim: Nearly half of media job losses over four years came from movie & sound recording, with written publishing next at more than 70k jobs lost.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Shows which media subsectors are taking the most labor damage.
insights.locator: Overall, nearly half the media job losses

insights.claim: Media job losses show no sign of slowing: they hover around 50k a year and have sped up in recent months.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: The trend is still running, not bottoming, so there's no recovery thesis yet for legacy media employment.
insights.quote: Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months.
insights.locator: Overall, nearly half the media job losses

insights.claim: Live broadcasting, streaming and graphic design are in an unusual downturn after years of stability, while publishing's decline continues a decades-long trend.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: The newly hit categories are the ones where AI's marginal effect is most likely.
insights.locator: Some of those digital job losses

insights.claim: Napster-era piracy undermined music copyrights and pushed down the value of individual songs until Spotify and Apple Music could consolidate catalogues and charge a trivial subscription fee.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: When copyright is diluted, value goes to aggregators and distributors, not content owners. It's a template for what AI may do to content.
insights.quote: Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.

insights.claim: Music streaming revenue is still below 1990s physical media sales even before adjusting for inflation.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: After a tech-driven deflation, total industry revenue may never get back to its old peak.
insights.quote: even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales.
insights.locator: The music industry has never returned

insights.claim: Recorded music became a loss leader for concerts and merch: tours got longer, venues bigger and ticket prices soared, and without that live revenue musicians' income would have collapsed.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Scarce, non-copyable live experiences take the economic value when digital content is commoditized. That's bullish for live events and ticketing.
insights.quote: Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.
insights.locator: The music industry has never returned

themes.theme: Video and Hollywood squeezed for attention

insights.claim: Unlike music, Hollywood has no live-concert equivalent to fall back on as AI and user-generated content flood the market for attention.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Studios face a structural squeeze with no obvious fallback revenue, so be cautious on legacy video media.
insights.quote: unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.
insights.locator: Today, the plethora of video options

insights.claim: Movie ticket sales ended last year 25% below their 2019 peak in nominal terms, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not made up the gap.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Even nominal revenue in video is shrinking. Streaming hasn't replaced the old revenue pools.
insights.quote: movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop.
insights.locator: Today, the plethora of video options

insights.claim: Earlier video technology shifts (broadcast, cable, physical media) each raised total watch time, so the industry did well; the streaming and social era instead created zero-sum competition for limited attention.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Disruption hurts incumbents when it splits a fixed pool of attention rather than growing it.
insights.quote: Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval.

insights.claim: The worst case for creative businesses under AI is a newspaper-style collapse: US newspapers once employed about half a million people, more than the entire oil industry, and payrolls are now down nearly 85% and still falling.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Gives a tail-risk benchmark for how far legacy media employment and revenue could fall.
insights.quote: Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping.
insights.locator: The actual worst-case scenario

insights.claim: Magazine publishers have cut 66% of staff since the 1990s, and book publishers have cut 40%.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Shows how much damage different print formats took in the internet transition.
insights.locator: The actual worst-case scenario

insights.claim: Newspapers collapsed through unbundling: box scores, stock prices and weather each moved to specialist websites, ad revenue moved to Google, social media broke news faster, and paywalled content was easily copied around.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: AI could unbundle content again and send economics to the aggregator layer.
insights.quote: newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead.

insights.claim: Consumer aversion to explicitly AI-generated content may not protect arts jobs, because AI is increasingly used in media in ways end consumers can't see.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: 'Human-made' branding is a weak moat if AI gets into production pipelines anyway.
insights.quote: AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer.

insights.claim: About 32% of workers in arts, entertainment and recreation use generative AI to some degree, versus 62% across all industries, which is still enough that nearly every major media project could involve AI.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Media is a below-average adopter, so adoption still has room to grow.

insights.so_what: Choosing not to adopt AI isn't a durable strategy for incumbents; competition forces adoption.

insights.claim: The arts are a small part of the economy; the movie industry's income profile is closer to eggs or bicycles than to healthcare or finance, so AI art mainly affects culture, not macro outcomes.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Creative-sector job losses won't move macro aggregates. Treat them as a leading indicator, not a macro driver.

insights.claim: Leading AI labs give low priority to generating art: Anthropic has basically never done image, video or music generation, and OpenAI dropped its Sora video platform to put limited compute to better use.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity pushes frontier labs toward higher-value uses (math, science, coding). Generative media is a lower-margin use of compute.

insights.claim: Tech is the clearest case of AI-driven job loss outside media: tech added nearly 300k jobs in 2022 but has lost jobs every year since, its longest labor-market downturn, as coding agents replace programmers.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Software labor demand is in structural decline, which matters for tech wages, IT services and AI coding-tool demand.
insights.quote: Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.

insights.claim: Outside a few narrow sectors, AI job displacement has been minor: unemployment is below the 2010s average, turnover is very low, and legal and engineering firms have been hiring.
insights.speaker: Joseph Politano
insights.so_what: Fears of broad white-collar AI displacement aren't yet showing up in aggregate labor data.

insights.claim: If AI's economic impact is large enough to justify the trillions investors are betting on it, the job disruption seen in media and tech will spread to the wider economy.

insights.so_what: Either AI capex is overpriced or broad labor disruption is coming. Both outcomes can't be avoided at once.
